outcomes.text: Describe the particle model for states of matter and changes of state.
Explain, with particles, the difference between physical and chemical changes.
Explain the limits of the particle model, which treats particles as inelastic spheres.
Describe how and why the atomic model changed over time (Dalton to Bohr, Geiger and Marsden).
Describe the atom as a small positive nucleus surrounded by negative electrons.
Recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules.
Recall the relative charges and masses of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Work out numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions from atomic and mass numbers.

units.title: Topic C2: Elements, compounds and mixtures

outcomes.text: Explain what purity means in science versus everyday use.
Use melting point data to tell pure from impure substances.
Calculate relative formula masses of species and within balanced equations.
Work out a compound's empirical formula from atom ratios or a diagram, and the reverse.
Explain that many useful materials are formulations of mixtures, such as alloys.
Describe and explain filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation and fractional distillation.
Suggest suitable purification techniques from information about the substances.
Describe paper and thin layer chromatography.
Recall that chromatography uses a stationary and a mobile phase, and separation depends on distribution between them.
Interpret chromatograms, including measuring Rf values.
Suggest chromatography methods to tell pure from impure substances.
Describe metals and non-metals and explain how their properties differ.
Explain how atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their place in the Periodic Table.
Explain how an element's position relates to its electron arrangement and atomic number.
Explain how elements' reactions relate to electron arrangement and atomic number.
Explain how atomic number refined Mendeleev's arrangement into the modern Periodic Table.
Describe and compare bonds in ionic compounds and simple molecules.
Explain bonding by electrostatic forces and transfer or sharing of electrons.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for simple covalent and binary ionic substances.
Describe limitations of different representations and models of bonding.
Recall that carbon forms four covalent bonds.
Explain how carbon's chains and rings give a vast range of organic compounds.
Explain properties of diamond, graphite, fullerenes and graphene from their structure and bonding.
Use energy transfers and bond or intermolecular force strengths to explain change-of-state temperatures.
Use data to predict states of substances under given conditions.
Explain how bulk properties of ionic, molecular, giant covalent, polymer and metal materials relate to their bonding.
Compare nano dimensions with atoms and molecules.
Describe the surface area to volume relationship for different-sized particles and its effect on properties.
Describe how nanoparticle properties relate to their uses.
Explain possible risks of some nanoparticulate materials.
Use symbols to write formulae of elements and simple covalent and ionic compounds.
Write formulae and balanced equations using conservation of mass, including half equations.
Write formulae and balanced equations from a supplied Periodic Table.
Use common ion formulae to deduce a compound's formula.
Construct balanced ionic equations.
Describe physical states using state symbols (s, l, g, aq).
Recall and use the Avogadro constant and the mole.
Explain how mass of a substance relates to moles, in both directions.
Recall and use the law of conservation of mass.
Explain mass changes in open systems during reactions using the particle model.
Deduce the stoichiometry of an equation from masses and explain the effect of a limiting reactant.
Use a balanced equation to calculate masses of reactants or products.
Tell endothermic from exothermic reactions by the temperature change of the surroundings.
Draw and label reaction profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Explain activation energy as the energy needed for a reaction to happen.
Calculate energy change of a reaction from bond-making and bond-breaking energies.
Explain oxidation and reduction as gain or loss of oxygen, identifying what is oxidised or reduced.
Explain oxidation and reduction as loss or gain of electrons.
Recall that acids give hydrogen ions in water and alkali solutions contain hydroxide ions.
Describe neutralisation as acid reacting with an alkali or base to make a salt and water.
Recognise aqueous neutralisation as hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to give water.
Recall that carbonates and some metals react with acids and write balanced equations.
Use and explain dilute, concentrated, weak and strong for acids.
Recall that pH measures relative acidity and alkalinity.
Describe neutrality, acidity and alkalinity by how hydrogen ion concentration sets the pH value.
Use the idea that a tenfold rise in hydrogen ion concentration lowers pH by one.
Describe techniques and apparatus used to measure pH.
Recall that metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and non-metals at the anode with inert electrodes.
Predict the products of electrolysis of molten binary ionic compounds.
Describe competing reactions in electrolysis of aqueous ionic solutions.
Describe electrolysis through the ions present and the electrode reactions, with half equations.
Describe electrolysis with inert and non-inert electrodes.

units.title: Topic C4: Predicting and identifying reactions and products

outcomes.text: Recall simple properties of Groups 1, 7 and 0.
Explain how group properties depend on outer electrons and predict trends down the group.
Recall general properties of transition metals and their compounds, with examples.
Predict reactions and reactivity of elements from their Periodic Table positions.
Explain how metal reactivity with water or acid relates to forming a positive ion.
Deduce an order of reactivity of metals from experimental results.

topics.title: C4.2 Identifying the products of chemical reactions

outcomes.text: Describe tests for oxygen, hydrogen, carbon dioxide and chlorine.
Describe tests for aqueous cations and anions.
Describe how to do a flame test.
Identify species from test results.
Interpret flame tests to identify lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper ions.
Describe the advantages of instrumental methods of analysis.
Interpret an instrumental result against a reference data set.

units.title: Topic C5: Monitoring and controlling chemical reactions

outcomes.text: Explain how concentration in mol/dm3 relates to solute mass and solution volume.
Explain how solute mass and solution volume relate to concentration.
Describe the technique of titration.
Relate the volume of a solution of known concentration to the volume or concentration of another.
Describe the relationship between moles of gas and volume.
Calculate gas volumes in reactions using the molar gas volume at room temperature and pressure.
Calculate the theoretical mass of product from a given mass of reactant.
Calculate percentage yield from actual yield.
Define the atom economy of a reaction.
Calculate atom economy for a desired product from the balanced equation.
Explain why a reaction pathway is chosen given data such as atom economy.
Suggest practical methods to find a reaction's rate.
Interpret rate graphs and their gradients.
Describe how temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area change rate.
Explain effects of temperature, concentration and pressure on rate through collision frequency and energy.
Explain the effect of solid piece size on rate through surface area to volume ratio.
Describe the characteristics of catalysts and their effect on rate.
Identify catalysts in reactions.
Explain catalytic action through activation energy.
Recall that enzymes are biological catalysts.
Recall that some reactions can be reversed by changing conditions.
Recall that dynamic equilibrium in a closed system means equal forward and reverse rates.
Predict how changing conditions shifts equilibrium and suggest conditions for maximum product.
Explain, using carbon's place in the reactivity series, how industry extracts metals.
Explain why and how electrolysis extracts some metals from ores.
Evaluate biological methods of metal extraction.
Explain the trade-off between rate and equilibrium position in processes like the Haber process.
Interpret graphs of reaction conditions against rate.
Explain how industrial conditions reflect raw material and energy cost, equilibrium and rate.
Explain the importance of the Haber process in agriculture.
Compare industrial and laboratory production of fertilisers.
Recall the importance of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium compounds in agriculture.
Describe industrial fertiliser production as several integrated processes.
Describe the principles of a life-cycle assessment.
Interpret data from a life-cycle assessment.
Describe how a material is recycled for another use and why this is viable.
Evaluate factors affecting recycling decisions.
Describe the composition of important alloys related to their properties and uses.
Describe corrosion and the conditions that cause it.
Explain how corrosion is prevented by barriers and sacrificial protection.
Compare physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals.
Explain how material properties relate to use and choose materials for a use.
Recognise functional groups and members of the same homologous series.
Name and draw displayed formulae of the first four alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids.
Predict formulae and structures of reaction products for homologous series members.
Recall that the generality of functional group reactions determines the reactions of organic compounds.
Recall the principles of addition polymerisation.
Deduce an addition polymer from its alkene monomer, and the reverse.
Explain the principles of condensation polymerisation.
Describe practical techniques to make a polymer by condensation.
Recall that DNA is a polymer of nucleotides and that other natural polymers are based on sugars and amino acids.
Describe separating crude oil by fractional distillation.
Explain this separation using molecular size and intermolecular forces.
Describe fractions as mixtures of alkanes of formula CnH2n+2.
Recall that crude oil is a hydrocarbon source and petrochemical feedstock.
Explain modern life's dependence on hydrocarbons and that crude oil is finite.
Describe cracking to make more useful materials.
Recall that a chemical cell gives a potential difference until reactants run out.
Evaluate hydrogen/oxygen and other fuel cells for given uses.

topics.title: C6.3 Interpreting and interacting with earth systems

outcomes.text: Interpret evidence for how the early atmosphere formed.
Describe how an oxygen-rich atmosphere developed.
Describe the greenhouse effect as radiation interacting with matter in the atmosphere.
Evaluate evidence for human causes of climate change and its uncertainties.
Describe effects of rising carbon dioxide and methane and how to mitigate them.
Describe sources of carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates and the problems they cause.
Describe the main ways to increase potable water supply using separation techniques.
